case_studies.title: GUIDE: Governed Unified Intelligence for Document-to-Artifact Generation in Enterprise Settings
case_studies.abstract: Enterprise guideline documents are heterogeneous and multimodal, combining narrative text, complex tables, and embedded images. Existing LLM and VLM systems face hallucinated content, table structure degradation, and lack governed workflows extending beyond extraction to validation and artifact generation. This leaves enterprises to perform this manually, consuming 2-3 days per document. To address this, we introduce GUIDE, a governed multi-agent framework built on a shared versioned rule store with schema-validated inter-agent contracts and end-to-end provenance tracking. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of extracting and validating data from complex enterprise documents, by building a governed framework called GUIDE that automates the process. The result is a significant reduction in manual effort, from 2-3 days per document to potentially near-instant generation. This research is not directly relevant to cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty: Guided multi-agent system could revolutionize document processing in large enterprises. IT Relevance: Directly affects enterprise document processing with potential to automate tasks. Value 90 Days: Immediate application possible with existing technology stacks.

case_studies.title: Towards Automated Domain Model Extraction from Source Code using Heuristics and Open-Source LLMs
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown strong capabilities for code understanding, making them promising for reverse engineering domain models from source code. However, state-ofthe- art proprietary LLMs cannot be used in many industrial contexts due to privacy and confidentiality constraints, while compact open-source LLMs that can run locally are limited by their context window and cannot process large code bases directly. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of extracting domain models from source code, building an automated approach using open-source large language models. The result is a method that can extract domain models from source code using locally deployable models. This could help with code understanding and reverse engineering in certain projects.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage legacy codebases, here is what to do: review this research for potential application in automating domain model extraction, assess the feasibility of integrating open-source LLMs into your workflow, and evaluate the benefits for your specific use case. This flags a risk: if your org relies on proprietary LLMs, check the privacy and confidentiality constraints immediately.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper is relevant to IT engineering and uses a specific deployment angle, but has some novelty that is largely academic and may not impact real-world work directly within 90 days.

case_studies.title: Beyond Trial-and-Error: Agentic Optimization for Image-to-Video Adherence
case_studies.abstract: Modern black-box Image-to-Video (I2V) models offer powerful capabilities in automated content creation, yet their lack of fine-grained control and reliability presents significant challenges in professional workflows. Their inherent stochasticity causes minor variations in textual prompts or hyperparameters to yield drastically different outputs often necessitating inefficient, brute-force trial-and-error processes. To address these limitations, we introduce the ``Agentic Self-Improvement" framework, which reframes video synthesis into a closed-loop, goal-directed optimization. Our framework s
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of unreliable outputs in Image-to-Video models by introducing a new framework called Agentic Self-Improvement, which optimizes video synthesis through a closed-loop process, resulting in more controlled and consistent outputs. The framework was built to address the limitations of current models, which often require trial-and-error processes. This research is focused on content creation and not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novel framework for optimizing image-to-video models could inspire agentic systems for automation or workflow optimization in IT infrastructure. However, direct IT relevance and business value are limited unless the concepts are applied to a real-world IT problem. This could score higher if the authors demonstrated its application in real-world IT scenarios.

case_studies.title: One Frozen Simulator Is Not Enough: Simulator Collapse in Multi-Agent RL
case_studies.abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning for human-AI interaction typically relies on a single large language model to simulate user behavior. We show that this approach systematically fails to generalize, and trace the failure to simulator collapse: because the simulator LLM is mode-collapsed, an LLM policy trained against it overfits to narrow strategies that exploit the simulator's dominant mode, and such a policy transfers poorly to unseen simulators and real users. We formalize this collapse theoretically and propose two complementary solutions, one at inference time and one at training time. T
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of simulator collapse in multi-agent reinforcement learning, where a single large language model fails to generalize user behavior. The authors built two complementary solutions to address this issue, one for inference time and one for training time. The result shows that these solutions can improve the generalization of policies in multi-agent reinforcement learning.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on reinforcement learning and language models, but IT consultants working with AI or machine learning teams may want to flag this as a potential area of research to explore for improving AI model generalization.
case_studies.score_reasoning: While this paper explores simulator collapse in multi-agent RL, which involves large language models, it does not reveal something directly surprising about tools or systems used by IT engineers. Its relevance to IT is also somewhat tangential (score 10). However, it does provide insights that could be useful for developers who deploy agentic systems. The value in 90 days is 10 for developers who can use the concepts to adjust their approaches and avert similar issues.

case_studies.title: No One to Blame: A Framework of Constitutive AI Unaccountability
case_studies.abstract: The increasing deployment of autonomous, agentic AI systems challenges traditional accountability mechanisms. Existing research predominantly frames AI accountability gaps as barriers that can be overcome through better standards, transparency, and institutional reform. We argue that this framing is insufficient: certain configurations of actors, systems, and institutions render AI accountability conceptually unachievable regardless of effort. case_studies.summary: This research identifies a problem with holding AI systems accountable for their actions, and the authors built a framework to understand when it's impossible to achieve accountability, resulting in a concept called constitutive AI unaccountability. The study found that certain AI system configurations make accountability unachievable. This concept is relevant to understanding AI system limitations.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI-infused cloud infrastructure, here is what to do: review your AI system configurations to identify potential unaccountability gaps, assess the risks associated with these gaps, and develop strategies to mitigate them. This flags a risk: if your organization uses autonomous AI systems, check your accountability mechanisms immediately. Not directly applicable to non-AI related IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper discusses the concept of constitutive AI unaccountability but has low IT relevance and no immediate practical application. The IT angle is related to deployment of autonomous, agentic AI systems, but it is discussed from a sociological perspective rather than an engineering or deployment-focused one.

case_studies.title: Is Per-Agent Policy Composition Safe? Rethinking Successor-Feature Transfer in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
case_studies.abstract: Many reinforcement learning systems, from fleet management to traffic signal control, must serve an objective that changes dynamically after deployment, and retraining a policy for each new objective is prohibitively expensive. For a single agent, this problem is well understood: successor features with generalized policy improvement, together with their universal extension, recombine a library of learned policies into a policy for any new objective, with a guarantee that the result is never worse than any policy in the library. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of retraining policies in multi-agent reinforcement learning systems when objectives change. The authors built a method to compose policies safely in cooperative multi-agent environments. The result shows that recombining learned policies can guarantee a policy that is never worse than any policy in the library.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on reinforcement learning in multi-agent systems, but may be relevant to organizations using AI and machine learning in areas like fleet management or traffic signal control.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Research is relevant to multi-agent reinforcement learning and its application in cooperative systems. Novelty in the multi-agent aspect. However, direct real-world impact is limited as it's mostly focused on academic understanding.

case_studies.title: Rethinking Agent Security as a Networking Problem
case_studies.abstract: AI agents are rapidly becoming more capable and widely deployed, promising substantial gains in productivity and enabling new classes of applications. However, their growing autonomy also introduces significant privacy and security risks. Existing defenses are predominantly agent-centric, relying on the agent itself to detect threats and enforce privacy and security policies. This approach is fundamentally limited because it entrusts policy enforcement to AI agents whose LLM-driven behavior is inherently nondeterministic and vulnerable to manipulation through attacks such as prompt injection.
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of security risks in AI agents by treating it as a networking problem, the authors built a new approach to enforce privacy and security policies, and the result shows that this approach can mitigate the risks of AI agent autonomy. The research focuses on the limitations of existing agent-centric defenses and proposes a new method to address these limitations. The authors aimed to improve the security of AI agents in various applications.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI agent deployments, here is what to do: review your current security policies, assess the risks of prompt injection attacks, and consider alternative approaches to policy enforcement that do not rely solely on the agent itself. This flags a risk: if your org uses AI agents with LLM-driven behavior, check your security controls immediately to ensure they are not vulnerable to manipulation. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work, but relevant to those managing AI agent deployments.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Directly relevant to IT security and infrastructure, but may require further reading to understand practical implications.

case_studies.title: TRACES: A Benchmark for Epistemic Reliability in Scientific Reasoning by LLMs
case_studies.abstract: Large language models are being proposed as agents in scientific workflows, in domains where no downstream verifier exists. Such deployment assumes the model can distinguish reliable scientific literature from unreliable literature, a capability that has not yet been directly measured. Existing benchmarks evaluate factuality on questions with known answers; the failure mode we target here is different. We introduce a probe corpus of 42 retracted, fraudulent, and pseudoscientific papers, paired with a methodology for eliciting and scoring single-shot model engagement with each paper's framing.
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating the reliability of scientific literature by large language models. The authors built a benchmark called TRACES to measure the ability of language models to distinguish between reliable and unreliable scientific papers. The result is a probe corpus that can be used to test language models, but it's not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: High novelty due to new benchmark, but IT relevance is low as it's a specific niche for scientific reasoning by LLMs. Value within 90 days is limited.

case_studies.title: Teaching a Large Language Model Tutor to Withhold the Answer: A Supervisor Architecture and an Evidence-Driven Method for Tuning Socratic Behavior
case_studies.abstract: An effective large language model (LLM) tutor must often decline to give an answer it could easily produce. In a randomized study, students who used an unguarded chatbot scored higher while practicing but lower on a later test taken without it, whereas a Socratically guarded version of the same model kept the practice gain and removed the later loss [4]. Reliable answer-withholding is therefore central to a tutor's value, yet a capable model pressed by a frustrated student does not withhold reliably on a prompt alone. We report a deployed tutoring system that enforces answer-withholding as a p
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of large language models giving away answers too easily, by building a supervisor architecture that can withhold answers, resulting in better learning outcomes for students. The system was tested and showed that students who used the Socratically guarded version of the model performed better on later tests. This research is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on the development of a tutoring system for educational purposes.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper's IT relevance is moderate, but novelty and value are limited. No immediate real-world application is apparent.

case_studies.title: The Role Specialization Model (RSM): Coordinating LLM-Based Tools in Agentic Software Development - An Exploratory Case Study
case_studies.abstract: The integration of large language models (LLMs) into software development workflows has given rise to a paradigm known as Agentic Software Engineering (SE 3.0), in which autonomous agents manage full development life cycles under human supervision. This paper presents an exploratory case study in which three LLM-based tools, Antigravity (an agentic IDE with a Gemini 2.5 backend), Gemini CLI, and Qwen Code (local execution via Ollama), are coordinated according to a role-distribution framework proposed in this work as the Role Specialization Model (RSM). Three research questions guide the study
case_studies.summary: This research explores how to coordinate tools using large language models in software development, the authors built a framework called the Role Specialization Model, and the result is a more efficient way to manage development life cycles. It aims to solve the problem of integrating autonomous agents into software development workflows. The study focused on coordinating three specific tools using this framework.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage software development infrastructure, this research may not directly impact your immediate work, but it flags a potential future risk: if your organization starts using large language models in development, you should be prepared to coordinate these tools efficiently, potentially using a framework like the Role Specialization Model.
case_studies.relevance_tag: LLM-based tools, Agentic Software Engineering, software development workflows
case_studies.score_reasoning: Presents a novel role specialization model for coordinating LLM-based tools, but lacks IT-specific deployment and practical usage. Directly relevant to future AI adoption in software workflows, but value in 90 days is limited.
